repost.content:
Ready to learn something awesome?

I've been playing with Databricks Lakebase lately and I'm impressed by some of the features that come with it. I mean, you can sync data from a Lakehouse to Lakebase (OLAP to OLTP) and vice versa using Lakebase CDF. But most importantly, I'm impressed by how Lakebase branching works.

Traditionally, setting up a new environment meant performing a dump of the data and waiting for that to finish. This could take minutes or hours or days (depending on the size of the data). Moreover, the data becomes stale the moment you start copying it; hence, your pipeline is being tested with older data when performing a full copy. Setting access, managing resources for the full replication, and the cost for storing the data are some other factors that make developers think before they create a new env.

Lakebase solves that problem with database branching. Database branching, unlike database copy, points to the same storage without copying anything. That means if you create a dev branch from prod, they point to the same schema and data at a specific point in time, share the same underlying storage without data duplication and data is stored only when changes happen. This is called copy-on-write.

So why is this possible now? Why isn't traditional Postgres able to do this? In a traditional pg server, the compute and storage are tightly coupled. The database process and the data live in the same instance. Hence, the only option is to perform a full copy of the data.

What Databricks has done is decouple the storage and compute, allowing data to be written to a versioned storage engine. This means that lakebase versions each change instead of overwriting it! Same concept as Delta tables. That also unlocks a powerful tool! Time Travelling!

Now, you can have a branch for each developer, each PR, and each test run. You can also create and delete these branches at your own convenience!

Databricks has consistently been solving complex data engineering problems, and this is one of the big ones!

How do you use Lakebase in your projects? Excited to know!

#lakebase #dataengineering #databricks

posts.content: Contextual policies is the way to go for managing the security of agents!

author.name: Ali Ghodsi
author.info: CEO & Co-Founder at Databricks, Adjunct Professor at UC Berkeley

postedAt.postedAgoText: 2 months ago • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn

repost.content:
Most coding agents have very limited features for controlling security: just a list of actions to allow, deny, or ask the user for. In Omnigent, we introduced Contextual Policies, which can track *state* about a session to manage both security and cost in a far more flexible way. You can add these over existing agents like Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode and custom agents you build yourself.

Tracking state makes policies way more powerful. Here are some examples of what you can do:
- Track whether an agent has read a confidential document, and if so, require human approval for it to send emails outside your org.
- Track the total cost of each agent session as it runs and ask the user to continue after each $10 spent, to avoid surprises when an agent does something expensive.
- Limit the impact of prompt-injection by tracking whether an agent has read untrusted external content.
- Compute a risk score for each agent based on the actions it took so far (e.g. reading external web pages, downloading software or accessing confidential docs might all increase risk), and use that to decide what actions to allow.
- Set agent permissions dynamically based on the first prompt the user sent. For example, if I ask the agent to create a Google Presentation for me, it should not be pushing code to GitHub.

Omnigent ships with many useful built-in policies in the open source repo and lets you write your own. Read more about contextual policies at  https://lnkd.in/gnvJkzsf

posts.content:
I’m going to continue embarrassing my co-founder Reynold. Our new engine is officially named after him. We’re calling it 𝐑𝐞𝐲𝐝𝐞𝐧, which stands for REYnold's Dream ENgine. 

The name comes from a question he posed to the team two years ago: Is it actually possible for the exact same engine to serve BI workloads at ultra-low latency AND handle massive-scale data warehousing?

After two years of relentless work by an amazing team of engineers, I believe the answer is yes.

For the last few decades, if you wanted real-time BI dashboards or real-time apps, you were forced to copy your data over to a completely separate, specialized engine. With Lakehouse-RT (powered by Reyden), you get millisecond latency directly on the warehouse.

Unlike every other approach out there: 
• You do not need to make a copy of the data . 
• It runs natively on open lakehouse formats like Iceberg. 
• Everything is governed by Unity Catalog.

To my knowledge, no other data warehouse can do these types of latencies without requiring a copy of the data. That is, an engine that can to complex large data joins and ultra low (10s ms) latency on that one copy directly.  No separate engine, no separate format. Just all of your data, super fast.
Link to the technical deep dive on Lakehouse-RT below.

repost.content:
Really excited to open source a new project: Omnigent, a meta-harness for AI agents. https://lnkd.in/g5QfG_aw 

It lets you build multi-agent coding and custom agents, sitting above Claude Code, Codex, Pi, and agent SDKs to let you compose them. It also adds live collaboration and rich control policies.

Omnigent is based on the trend we saw with AI usage at Databricks and Neon: engineers were combining multiple agents into loops and workflows, and this was difficult above the harness layer. We add a uniform API above any harness that enables rich features on top.

For composition, it lets you create multi-agent teams with different harnesses or swap harness and model mid-session and mid-loop.

For collaboration, Omnigent adds a common UI above any agents, with native app, web and mobile UIs and live collaboration with teammates. No more copy-pasting text and screenshots between agents, Slack, and Docs!

For security & cost control, Omnigent introduces a *contextual* policy model that can track session state  (e.g. ask for permission to git push if an agent downloaded an untrusted npm package, or ask you after every $100 of spend) and a strong OS sandbox from our security team.

We think a lot of work will move beyond the individual agent level and to a meta-harness layer like this as agents get more widely adopted, so we're very excited to open source our foundation for it, based on our needs for coding and custom agents at Databricks and Neon.

I'm doing all my coding, and product management in this now and love having a single interface to all my agents. Try it out and join the open source community to contribute!
